exam: A 45‑year‑old man with epigastric pain improves after meals – what is the most likely ulcer type and why? — Duodenal ulcer; pain relief with food suggests duodenal location where acid is buffered.
You have no endoscopy; how do you confirm H. pylori infection? — Use stool antigen or urea breath test; both detect active infection.
Patient presents with melena and low blood pressure; what is your immediate management? — Stabilise haemodynamics, give IV fluids, arrange urgent endoscopy or surgical review.
Why is clarithromycin contraindicated in this region? — High local macrolide resistance reduces eradication success; alternative antibiotics are preferred.
Explain the sequence from chronic gastritis to gastric cancer in H. pylori infection. — Chronic inflammation → atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma.
A patient on long‑term NSAIDs develops dyspepsia; how does H. pylori status affect management? — Test and treat for H. pylori; eradication reduces ulcer risk and may allow continuation of NSAIDs.

What are the key differences between a gastric and duodenal ulcer on endoscopy? — Gastric ulcer: located in stomach, margins often irregular, may have surrounding erythema; duodenal ulcer: in duodenal bulb, clean base, less surrounding inflammation.
How would you manage H. pylori infection in a pregnant woman? — Use a regimen avoiding tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones; amoxicillin‑based triple therapy is preferred.
ai.title: Helicobacter pylori Infection
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Helicobacter pylori is a common gastric bacterium causing chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer. Diagnosis relies on non‑invasive tests or endoscopy, and eradication therapy is essential.

b: Transmitted mainly oral‑fecal; prevalence >70% in many low‑resource settings
Key virulence factors: urease, CagA, VacA
sections.p: H. pylori colonises the gastric mucosa, surviving acidic pH by producing urease. It induces inflammation that can progress to ulceration or malignancy.

b: Chronic gastritis → atrophic changes → intestinal metaplasia → cancer
Duodenal ulcer more common in younger patients; gastric ulcer in older patients
Co‑infection with malaria or schistosomiasis may blunt inflammatory response
sections.p: Clinical disease depends on bacterial load, host genetics, and co‑morbidities such as HIV or chronic NSAID use.

b: Epigastric burning improves with meals (duodenal ulcer) or worsens (gastric ulcer)
Unexplained weight loss or early satiety raises suspicion for malignancy
sections.p: Patients present with epigastric pain, dyspepsia or bleeding. In low‑resource hospitals, endoscopy may be unavailable, so clinicians rely on symptom patterns and simple tests.

t.b: Detects active infection; positive result confirms H. pylori
Detects current infection; useful when breath test unavailable

t.a: Rapid urease test on biopsy (if endoscopy performed)
t.b: Provides immediate result; positive indicates bacterial urease activity
Shows past exposure; not reliable for active infection, but useful where other tests absent

b: Check for melena, hematemesis, or orthostatic hypotension
Palpate for epigastric tenderness; peritoneal signs suggest perforation
sections.p: Focus on history of dyspepsia, NSAID use, and risk factors for ulcer complications. Physical exam often normal; look for signs of bleeding.

b: Assuming a negative serology rules out active infection
Prescribing clarithromycin in areas with high macrolide resistance without susceptibility data
sections.p: Avoid treating dyspepsia empirically without confirming infection in high‑prevalence areas, and never give PPIs alone for ulcer disease without addressing H. pylori.

whenToSeekHelp: Perforated ulcer (sudden severe abdominal pain, rigid abdomen)
Upper GI bleed with haemodynamic instability
Persistent vomiting with inability to tolerate oral medication
